paper_title: AdaExploreBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Proactive Exploration and Test-time Adaptation in Evolving Environments

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents in unfamiliar and partially observable interactive environments (Du et al., 2026). In such settings, agents often cannot rely on given observations, but must actively interact with the unknown environment to collect evidence necessary to successfully resolve tasks being presented to them (He et al., 2025). This requires proactive exploration: deciding when, what, and how much to interact for understanding the surrounding *Equal Contribution. 1 environment (Wang et al., 2025; Jhamtani et al., 2025). The challenge becomes harder when the environment is constantly evolving (Chen et al., 2025a). Previously acquired evidence may become stale as the underlying dynamics change, requiring the agent to recognize and re-explore (Chen et al., 2025a; Yoo et al., 2024). We refer to this capability as adaptive exploration: the ability to detect, reexplore and revise in response to environmental dynamics (Sun et al., 2023). This ability is particularly important for test-time adaptation in evolving environments, where hypothesis that were valid earlier may become stale during deployment (Lucas and Jurgovsky, 2020; Gama et al., 2014). However, as summarized in Table 1, existing benchmarks do not fully capture these capabilities. The evidence are often given (Hua et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026a) or leaked from environment (Liu et al., 2026c), and the environments are often stationary (He et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026b). These limitations motivate our central question: Can LLM agents proactively explore to understand and adapt to the environmental dynamics? Answering the question needs benchmark with: (1) Self-directed environment exploration, where agents must actively gather evidence to uncover environmental rules, rather than relying on provided evidence or predefined task-completion objectives; and (2) Unannounced environmental changes, where latent rules may shift without explicit notification, requiring agents to recognize when previously acquired knowledge becomes outdated and re-explore to adapt. To this end, we introduce AdaExploreBench, benchmark for proactive exploration and testtime adaptation in evolving environments. In this work, we instantiate environmental dynamics as latent rules, mapping from agents action to its outcome (Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024). Understanding the rules corresponds to learning the environment, while change in the rule represents Benchmark / Work Proactive Exploration Adaptive Exploration Env-learning Exploration In-Process Evaluation Heterogeneous Rules Scalable Generation InductionBench (Hua et al., 2025) HEROS JOURNEY (Zheng et al., 2026a) RULEARN (He et al., 2025) NewtonBench (Zheng et al., 2026b) WILT (Banatt et al., 2024) OdysseyArena (Xu et al., 2025) CausalGame (Chen et al., 2026b) ExplorationBench (Zhang et al., 2026) PhysGym (Chen et al., 2025b) AdaPlanBench (Liu et al., 2026c) PlanBench-XL (Liu et al., 2026a) AdaExploreBench (Ours) Table 1: Positioning of AdaExploreBench. For each work, the table reports whether each trait is fully (), partially () or not () addressed. Detailed explanations of each terminology are provided in Appendix A. evolving environments. AdaExploreBench consists of 256 evaluation and 1000 training instances over four rule families. In the default setting, the agent decides itself on when to interact, which input values to query, and how many evidence to collect. Meanwhile, unannounced rule drift occurs during interaction, where agents must detect from altered exploration outcome. To ensure that even agents with limited exploration effort have opportunities to recognize rule drift, evaluation cases are presented sequentially in small batches. Agents can thus detect rule drift through either further exploration or performance degradation. This protocol also yields performance curve over the interaction, enabling in-process evaluation for further analysis. We evaluate eight leading LLMs on AdaExploreBench. Our results suggest that proactive exploration and test-time adaptation remains highly challenging. While all models get below 70% calibrated accuracy in default setting , giving extra evidence or removing rule changes improves average performance by 9.4% and 6.2% significantly, suggesting that models are considerably better at exploiting given evidence in static environment. We further find that exploration quality is more important than quantity, and agents often report partially correct but incomplete rules and rule changes. Thess findings show that current LLM agents still lag in proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environment. We summarize our main contributions as: Scalable Construction Pipeline: We introduce AdaExploreBench, scalable LLM-based generation pipeline to synthesize complex and diverse evaluation instances without extra human labor. Evolving Environment Design: We instantiate proactive and adaptive exploration in an evolving environment governed by latent rules and rule changes, reflecting real-world challenges and providing testbed for future training. Thorough Analysis: We evaluate eight LLMs and reveal that current agents remain limited in proactive exploration and dynamic adaptation. Together, our work provides foundation for understanding the limitations of current LLM agents and serves as training playground for improving their exploration and adaptation capabilities.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Proactive Exploration for Environment Learning. Recent work moves beyond reasoning over given evidence by letting agents proactively explore to learn the environment. Prior work studies proactive learning through scientific discovery (Zheng et al., 2026b), interactive learning (He et al., 2025), hypothesis testing (Banatt et al., 2024), long-horizon induction (Xu et al., 2025), and alienworld exploration (Zhang et al., 2026). These works test proactive exploration and targeted at environment learning, but the environment typically remains static, and sometimes leaks information not queried by the agent (He et al., 2025). In contrast, AdaExploreBench prevents information leakage and introduces unannounced rule drift, requiring agents to re-explore and adapt accordingly. Test-time Adaptation. complementary line of work studies adaptation when task-relevant conditions change during interaction. Related work studies adaptation to changing conditions through concept drift (Gama et al., 2014), deployment-time dynamics grounding (Chen et al., 2026a), progressively revealed constraints (Liu et al., 2026c), unreliable tools (Liu et al., 2026a), and changing tool 2 Figure 1: Overview of AdaExploreBench. However, these works emphasize statistical adaptation or task-oriented replanning, whereas AdaExploreBench requires agents to recognize unannounced rule drift, revise their hypotheses, and proactively re-explore. sections.title: 3.1 Data Generation
sections.content: Definitions. We consider decision-making environments where an agent selects actions based on observable input fields. Each case contains set of field values, and the agent chooses from four actions = {a0, a1, a2, a3} ordered by intervention strength. subset of fields, termed factors, determines the appropriate intervention, with each factor having positive or negative directional effect. The latent environmental dynamics map each case to an intervention score [1, 1], where higher scores favor stronger interventions. fixed utility function maps this score to action utilities, rewarding actions whose intervention levels better match the score. An episode is complete evaluation instance comprising task and sequence of cases governed by potentially changing environmental dynamics. Task Specification. Each task defines an operational scenario, an agent role, and four ordered actions based on predefined blueprints across finance, healthcare, cybersecurity, and manufacturing. We use LLM-assisted generation to construct field catalog with semantic descriptions, numerical ranges, and sampling distributions. Each episode selects relevant factors and irrelevant distractors from the catalog. We further impose (1) cross-field constraints to ensure feasible field combinations and (2) dynamics constraints to specify admissible factor interactions and environmental changes. Environmental Dynamics. We instantiate four families representing different decision-making strategies (Einhorn, 1970; Payne et al., 1993). Additive dynamics aggregate evidence across factors, conjunctive and disjunctive dynamics require all or any conditions to be satisfied, and lexicographic dynamics follow factor priority order. The resulting evidence is calibrated to common intervention score. In static settings, the underlying dynamics remain fixed, while dynamic settings introduce an unannounced rule drift that replaces one relevant factor and reverses another factors direction within the same family. These changes are constrained to be semantically plausible and induce meaningful yet moderate shifts in optimal actions. Detailed formalizations are provided in Appendix C. Episode Generation and Validation. We construct episodes by instantiating latent dynamics and sampling feasible evaluation cases using established field catalog and following the constraints. Candidates undergo structural, numerical, and semantic validation to ensure valid configurations, non-degenerate action distributions, and plausible environmental changes. further LLM-based review evaluates field realism, change plausibility, and distractor quality. We retain only qualified episodes from candidates for the final benchmark. Detailed procedures and prompts are provided in Appendix D. To ensure high quality, human study of the generated instances are given in Appendix E.

sections.title: 3.2 Runtime Protocol
sections.content: Interaction Protocol. At the beginning of each episode, the agent receives the task description, input fields and ranges, available actions, definitions of the four dynamics families, and interaction tools. The instantiated family, relevant factors, parameters, and occurrence and timing of environmental changes remain hidden. Each episode proceeds through evaluation batches preceded by exploration windows. The agent may use Probe Batch to query self-designed cases and observe utilities for all actions, or Request Next Batch to proceed without probing. For each revealed evaluation batch, Submit Action Batch collects action choices and returns utility feedback. Calculator supports numerical reasoning. The agent decides whether, what, and how much to explore, while receiving cumulative utility feedback throughout the episode. Evaluation History Masking. By default, completed evaluation cases and selected actions are removed from subsequent context, while their realized utilities remain available. In contrast, selfcollected probe observations are retained. This isolates proactive exploration from environmentprovided evidence while preserving non-diagnostic feedback that may signal environmental changes. Auxiliary Assessment. We conduct necessary assessments to directly evaluate whether agents identify relevant factors, their directional effects, and changes in environmental dynamics. Assessments are collected immediately before rule drift and at episode completion in dynamic settings, and only at completion in static settings. They are excluded from subsequent interaction context to avoid influencing agent behavior. Please refer to Appendix for detailed and additional runtime settings.

sections.title: 4.1 Settings
sections.content: Models. Our evaluation includes proprietary and leading open-source models with distinct parameter scale. Proprietary models include GPT-6-Luna, GPT-6-Sol (OpenAI, 2026), and Gemini-3.8-Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026), while open-source models include DeepSeek-V4.1Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), Gemma-4-12B (Team, 2026), Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a), and Qwen3.827B (Qwen Team, 2026b). Detailed reasoning and inference configs are specified in Appendix G. Experimental Settings. Each setting is combination of configurations of (1) Whether rule drift occur. (2) Whether evaluation batches are masked. (3) Whether probings are mandatory. We evaluate agents under the following settings: (1) Default. rule drift occurs during interactions. Evaluation batches are masked. Probing amount is self-decided by the agent. (2) Stationary. The same as default except that rule drift does not occur during interactions. (3) Evidence Given. The same settings as default except that Evaluation batches are not masked. (4) Forced-Probe. The same settings as default except that probings are mandatory in every window with minimal number of cases required. We evaluate the main results under default setting and the other settings are for analysis.

sections.title: 4.2 Metrics
sections.content: We evaluate end-to-end performance, exploration behavior and adaptation performance. The detailed metrics definitions are provided in Appendix H. Each evaluation case receives credit only when the agent selects the optimal action with largest utility feedback. We report the mean credit over evaluation cases. (2) Calibrated Accuracy (CA) is the calibrated version of EA, where near-optimal choices are granted partial credit based on the actual utility received. The score is further calibrated so that uniformly random policy obtains zero in expectation and the optimal policy obtains full score. (3) Mean Unique Probes measures the amount of exploration. sections.title: 4.3 Results
sections.content: Takeaway 1 Proactive and adaptive exploration remains highly challenging for most models. All models fall below 70% calibrated accuracy, and weaker models select more costly actions. Table 2 shows clear performance divide across models. Gemini-3.8-Flash achieves the strongest end-to-end performance, but still score below 70%. Moreover, the gap between EA and CA widens substantially as model performance decreases. It ranges from about 2 to 5 points for the top three models, but grows to 8 to 22 points for the remaining models. This suggests that weaker agents not only make incorrect decisions more frequently, but their mistakes also tend to incur larger utility losses. The results highlight the difficulty of proactive and adaptive exploration under evolving environments. Takeaway 2 Greater exploration and verification effort do not necessarily translate into better endto-end performance across models. Exploration effort yields highly unequal returns across models. Table 2 reveals variation in exploration behavior, with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash issuing approximately 24 times as many probes as Llama3.1-8B. However, this variation does not translate into proportional performance gains. Despite probing the most, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash achieves lower CA than both Gemini-3.8-Flash and GPT-6-Sol. Similarly, Gemini-3.8-Flash outperforms GPT-6Sol with fewer probes. These contrasts reveal discrepancy between exploration volume and realized performance, as models with fewer interactions can achieve substantially better outcomes. Additional verification does not close the performance gap. This discrepancy extends to postchange exploration. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash performs considerably more re-probes than the two strongest models, yet still achieves lower end-toend performance. Thus, additional opportunities to verify previously learned relationships do not lead to more successful adaptation. Together, these results highlight the limitations of measuring exploration through interaction counts alone and underscore the importance of evaluating how effectively agents acquire and exploit informative evidence. Takeaway 3 Adaptation ability distinguishes effective agents more clearly than exploration efforts. Recognition is stronger indicator of end-to-end performance. sections.content: Section 4.3 reports models behaviors under default setting. Here we ask why they fail by ablations. Rule Drift Adaptation. How much of the performance gap does rule drift cause? Evidence Sufficiency. How much is caused by the burden of acquiring evidence proactively? Exploration Quantity vs. Quality. Can forcing agents to explore more close the gap? Figure 2 reports Calibrated Accuracy (CA) for Default and the three diagnostic settings. Takeaway 4 Removing unannounced rule drift significantly recovers agents end-to-end outcome. barely help agents that cannot even learn in stationary setting. Rule Drift is thus first-order bottleneck for models with basic learning competence. Takeaway 5 Agents exploit effectively when sufficient evidence is provided externally. Most models improve substantially when sufficient evidence is given. The Evidence Given setting let passive evidence accumulate across batches. Six of the seven models improve, four by more than 15 CA points. The resulting gains identify proactive evidence acquisition as key bottleneck: models learn better from available evidence than they acquire it on their own. Qwen3.8-27B is the only model that degrades under Evidence Given, but it also cuts exploration effort the most as shown in Appendix I. This shows that sufficient given evidence that become stale later can mislead models that trust them without re-verifying, consistent with the near-zero re-probing effort in this setting. Takeaway 6 Effective exploration depends more on explored evidence quality than quantity. Removing rule drift recovers performance significantly for most models. The Stationary setting only removes rule drift compared with default setting. It raises CA by up to 14.7% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in Figure 2, and 6.2% on average. Though GPT-6-Sol barely changes, it is because its default performance is already near its stationary ceiling, consistent with its second-best Change Recognition in Table 2. The weakest models improves by less 1%, so removing rule drift Forcing agents to explore more barely help. If the gap reflected exploration willingness or amount, Forced-Probe should close it. In forced-probe setting, probing quantity indeed shifts drastically. As shown in Appendix I, Mean unique probes rise from 33.9 to 53.8 across all models, and the most reluctant explorers scale up their efforts by two to five times. Re-probes after the rule change also rise substantially. Yet performance stays flat or even degrades, with mean CA change of 2.0%. 6 Figure 3: Calibrated Accuracy per evaluation batch under default, with batch 0 marking the last pre-change batch. Probe informativeness emerges as likely bottleneck. Poor performance may stem from insufficient exploration effort, weak induction from available evidence, or uninformative probe selection. However, Forced-Probe weakens the first explanation, as increasing exploration effort fails to improve performance, while Evidence Given weakens the second, as models improve substantially when sufficient evidence is provided. Together, these findings suggest that the inability to select informative probe cases is key remaining bottleneck, although probe quality is not directly measured. Synthesis. Agents learn well from given evidence, but they neither acquire comparably useful evidence on their own, nor detect and revise around rule drift. The binding constraints on current LLM agents in evolving environments are proactive exploration quality and test-time adaptation, not exploration quantity or basic rule learning. More ablation studies are provided in Appendix J.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Simplified Environmental Dynamics. We model environmental dynamics as latent rules and rule drift, providing controlled but necessarily simplified abstraction of real-world environments. While this formulation cannot fully capture real-world complexity and uncertainty, agents already struggle with proactive exploration and adaptation even in these simplified settings. Indirect Assessment of Exploration Quality. Our exploration metrics primarily measure effort rather than quality. We omit direct quality metrics based on spatial diversity or decision-region coverage, as they inherently favor extensive probing and yield incomparable scores across heterogeneous rule families. Instead, we use corresponding ablations settings to indirectly examine whether ineffective evidence acquisition limits performance. Limited Coverage of Environmental Changes. Our evaluation currently focuses on within-family rule drift involving factor replacement and direction reversal. Due to time and computational resource constraints, we leave cross-family changes, alternative change types, and systematically varying change magnitudes for future work.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: Offensive Content. AdaExploreBench consists of synthetically generated scenarios across domains. The evaluation instances are constructed without collecting sensitive user data. The benchmark is designed solely for research evaluation and does not involve offensive content. Licenses. Evidence should be mostly self-queried, instead of given or leaked from the environment. Figure 4: Motivation of AdaExploreBench. An agent proactively explore and get confused when rule changes. Adaptive Exploration. The environment dynamics change during interaction without notifications, and the agent must detect the shift and explore again. Env-learning Exploration. Exploration aims to learn how the environment works, rather than to complete predefined task. In-Process Evaluation. Performance is measured throughout exploration instead of only at the end, yielding performance curve over the whole interaction process. Heterogeneous Rules. Latent rules span structurally and cognitively distinct families rather than variations of similar forms. sections.title: C Environment Formalization
sections.content: Rule families. The four rule families correspond to four common attribute-combination strategies: Additive. Relevant fields are combined through weighted sum. high value on one field can compensate for low value on another (Payne et al., 1993). Conjunctive. All relevant fields must satisfy their conditions. single field that falls below its threshold can limit the overall outcome (Einhorn, 1971). Disjunctive. Satisfying any one relevant condition can be sufficient. Thus, one strong field may determine the outcome even when other fields are weak (Einhorn, 1970). Lexicographic. Relevant fields are checked in fixed priority order. The highest-priority field is considered first, and lower-priority fields matter only when earlier fields are not decisive (Payne et al., 1993; Gigerenzer and Goldstein, 1996). Figure 5 illustrates the structural difference among the four families: additive rules aggregate evidence, conjunctive rules require all conditions, disjunctive rules require any condition, and lexicographic rules follow priority order. sections.title: D Data Generation Details
sections.content: D.1 Semantic Field Catalog Construction Catalog Specifications. The semantic field catalog is constructed using predefined schema and task blueprints. Each blueprint specifies the task scenario, agent role, and four ordered actions, while the schema defines the required field attributes, rule-family specifications, cross-field constraints, 13 and admissible environmental changes. LLMassisted synthesis extends these predefined specifications with task-specific field semantics and numerical parameters. Component Synthesis. For each task blueprint, we construct the semantic field catalog through the following component-level generation steps: Field Discovery. The LLM proposes set of candidate observable fields relevant to the task scenario, including field names, descriptions, units, and basic directional information. Field Semantics. For each retained field, the LLM specifies its applicability to different rule families, directional effects on intervention decisions, and admissible direction reversals with corresponding semantic events. Field Parameters. The LLM assigns numerical ranges, sampling distributions, and associated parameters to the accepted fields, establishing the field population used for subsequent episode generation. Lexicographic Orders. Based on the established field set, the LLM generates admissible priority orders for lexicographic decision rules. Cross-Field Constraints. The LLM defines feasibility constraints among fields to exclude invalid or contradictory combinations of field values. Cross-Field Dynamics. The LLM specifies admissible field replacement relations, including replacement groups, directional transitions, and coupling relationships for dynamic episodes. Detailed generation prompts and output specifications are provided in Appendix D.5. Validation and LLM Audit. Each generated component undergoes programmatic validation against the predefined schema and componentspecific constraints, followed by LLM-based semantic auditing. Components failing these checks are revised and revalidated or rejected. Crosscomponent consistency is further verified to ensure valid field references and compatible semantic specifications. Only accepted components are integrated into the finalized semantic field catalog for subsequent episode generation. D.2 Episode Generation Episode generation consists of two steps: searching for valid field and rule configurations, followed by sampling evaluation cases and organizing them into batches. ation batches. All cases are evaluated under the same latent dynamics. D.2.1 Field Configuration Search Candidate Enumeration. For each task and rule family, we enumerate candidate combinations of rule-relevant fields from the semantic field catalog. The enumeration follows seed-determined bounded traversal of the admissible combinations. For dynamic episodes, candidates additionally incorporate admissible field replacements and direction reversals. Configurations violating cross-field feasibility or rule applicability constraints are discarded before numerical evaluation. Numerical Certification. For each structurally valid configuration, we instantiate the corresponding latent dynamics and evaluate their properties over the feasible case population. Static candidates are calibrated and checked for non-degenerate optimal-action distributions. Dynamic candidates undergo three stages of numerical certification: initial screening, refinement, and held-out verification, using 256, 2048, and 16384 sampled cases, respectively. We evaluate the preand post-transition dynamics under shared calibration, requiring adequate action coverage, moderate changes in optimal-action assignments, and feasible target action transitions. Specifically, the natural rate of changed optimal actions is constrained to 0.25 0.75, with marginal optimal-action proportions between 0.15 and 0.35. Semantic Review. After numerical certification, additional distractor fields are selected to complete the observable field configuration. An LLM-based reviewer then assesses the semantic consistency of the selected fields and environmental dynamics with the task scenario. Candidates with invalid field configurations are rejected. Algorithm 1 summarizes the construction procedure, and the review prompt specification are provided in Appendix D.5. D.2.2 Evaluation Case Sampling For each accepted configuration, evaluation cases are sampled from the specified field distributions. The applicable latent dynamics determine the action utilities U(Rθ(x)), and the resulting cases are organized into evaluation batches. Static Setting. For static episodes, we independently sample cases from the field distributions conditioned on the cross-field feasibility constraints, and randomly organize them into evaluDynamic Setting. For dynamic episodes, we first sample shared pre-transition prefix under the initial dynamics, followed by multiple post-transition branches. The post-transition sampling includes an IID control branch drawn from the feasible case population and several targeted branches with specified optimal-action change rates. For each targeted branch, cases are sampled from pre/post actiontransition groups identified during numerical certification to achieve the desired change rate. The resulting branches share the same pre-transition cases but differ in their post-transition case distributions. Algorithm 2 summarizes the evaluation case sampling and batch assembly procedure. D.3 Dataset-Level Review and Selection After episode generation, separate LLM-based quality review evaluates each candidate along three dimensions: field realism, plausibility of dynamic rule transitions, and distractor quality. Episodes must exceed the minimum score threshold on every dimension to qualify for selection. Qualified episodes are ranked by their aggregate review scores within each domainrule-family combination, and equal numbers are selected from these groups to maintain dataset balance. The selected episodes form the final evaluation dataset. Detailed review criteria and prompts are provided in Appendix D.5. D.4 Dataset Configuration Dataset Composition. Our evaluation dataset consists exclusively of dynamic episodes, balanced across all domainrule-family combinations. We generate 384 candidate episodes, with 24 per combination, and retain the 256 highest-scoring qualified episodes through the dataset-level review and selection procedure, yielding 16 episodes per combination. Evaluation Batches. Each episode contains 12 action batches, with 8 evaluation cases per batch. The rule drift occurs after batch 5, 6, or 7, with the preceding batches shared across all post-transition branches. We construct one IID control branch and three targeted branches with optimal-action change rates of 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75. Each complete trajectory contains 96 evaluation cases. sections.content: Runtime configs. Table 6 lists the runtime configuration shared by every model and episode. Each episode presents its evaluation cases as fixed sequence of batches, and rule drift is scheduled after batch drawn approximately uniformly from the middle of that sequence. Within each batch window the agent may probe at most once, each probe call is capped in size, and probing is always optional because the upcoming batch can also be revealed directly. Every value is fixed across episodes, models, and settings. The fallbacks that apply once limit is exhausted are described in the text. before the environment applies the fallbacks described above; provider failures are retried with capped exponential backoff, and an over-length response is regenerated once before its window is skipped. These limits are identical for all models, and no model profile overrides them. Runtime Failure Handling. We distinguish protocol errors from provider failures. (1) Repair. Invalid agent responses, including malformed JSON, schema violations, and invalid tool calls, trigger an error message in the agents context and one additional interaction for correction, without advancing the environment. If the repair fails, the current exploration window is skipped, or unanswered evaluation cases receive zero utility and are counted as incorrect. Mandatory probing requirements are waived for the affected window. (2) Retry. Provider and network failures are retried with capped exponential backoff, without affecting the agents interaction history or repair budget. Exhausted retries mark the run as failed. Truncated responses receive one additional generation attempt, after which repeated truncation triggers the corresponding fallback. Runtime Prompts. Figure 16 shows the initial prompt that opens every episode under Default, and Figures 17, 18, 19, and 20 show the environment feedback that answers each of the four interaction tools. Angle brackets mark content that varies across episodes, such as the role assignment, the action names, and the field descriptions, while ellipses and bracketed elision notes stand for entries that repeat displayed structure. When an episode defines feasibility constraints, they appear as constraint list after the field descriptions in the first user message. Every environment message ends with the latest Current state card, which is the authoritative snapshot of tool usability, cumulative utility, pending cases, and remaining action batches. Request Next Batch call is answered through this card alone, because revealing batch without probing produces no separate result payload. After each submitted action batch, the environment rewrites the retained history as described in the system message, so later turns observe the scoreboard form of earlier outcomes instead of the original messages. Feedback for rejected calls is omitted from these figures, since rejection only triggers repair opportunity and leaves the episode state unchanged.

sections.title: Field Discovery Prompt
sections.content: You build the complete practical inventory of numeric measurements that support decision making in the supplied operational scenario. Return every realistic measurement that can realistically inform intervention tendency. Explore current state, exposure, workload, time, quality, exceptions, risk, recovery, forecasts, trends, completed historical evidence, and decision-relevant subgroups when they answer materially different operational questions; Give diverse set while preventing same or synonymous fields. Include an action-neutral numeric measurement when it describes or predicts the governed conditions expected loss, deterioration, urgency, or autonomous recovery within the decision horizon. It may describe the governed item or causally relevant route, cohort , queue, environment, or system. Exclude pure regime selectors, action authorization or execution capability, consequences of choosing stronger action, action-conditional forecasts, and the unresolved governed items post-decision outcome. For every field, output only stable field_id, concise display_name, integer or decimal type, exact unit, one concise description, and pressure_direction. The description must identify exactly one decision-evidence quantity and explain what the reported numeric value represents. To avoid ambiguity, you should make necessary clarifications as follows: When needed to distinguish the quantity, name the operands and their order for difference; the numerator, denominator, and time basis for fraction or rate; the target event and horizon for probability or forecast; and the governed population, observation window, and aggregation for cohort statistic. For field whose value may be not existing under certain circumstances, state it as undefined or null, but do not assign value that may cause ambiguity. For instance, for field "preparation_time", when there is no preparation at all, the value does not exist, state it as null/ undefined instead of assigning 0, else there could be ambiguity for preparation_time=0 ( do not know whether there is preparation but finished immediately or there is no preparation). For any one fixed surrounding decision condition, every retained field must have welldefined monotonic direction across its full defined legal numeric domain (do not need to consider situations where the field is undefined or unavailable). The direction must remain stable while that condition is fixed (but it may be different under another fixed condition). Across the fields entire legal domain, increasing the value must consistently support either the same or stronger intervention, or the same or weaker intervention; the direction must never switch within that domain. Omit field whose middle values are preferable while both lower and higher extremes require stronger intervention, or whose direction otherwise changes merely because its own value crosses threshold. While each field should have clear intervention tendency within one certain condition, the direction are allowed to flip across different regime. During discovery, actively and broadly look for fields whose entire monotonic direction could genuinely reverse after concrete, scenario-plausible event or condition change. For instance, "machine uptime minutes" normally means more availability and less intervention pressure, but during mandated preventive-shutdown window the same high uptime means the required outage was skipped, which requests for more intensive intervention. So do not limit your discover only to those fields who obviously point towards an adverse or intervention needs, deliberately brainstorm for independently useful, action-neutral direct measurements, such as direct operational levels, signed flows or rates, progress or completion, throughput, uptime or availability, elapsed or remaining time, neutral forecasts or trends, whose pressure direction is clear under the ordinary condition but may reverse after separate external event or condition change. Assign pressure_direction according to the fields ordinary interpretation in the recurring decision, if you consider field to be reversible, then it may have different direction under different circumstances, assign the direction for the most common situation you think: use 1 when increasing values monotonically support stronger intervention and -1 when increasing values monotonically support weaker intervention. Notice that we require the pressure_direction to be applied to the whole domain under one specific circumstances. plausible conditional reversal does not make the base pressure_direction ambiguous. Also consider distinct measurements that could both serve the same decision role when concrete workflow event changes which measurement is valid evidence, where they could potentially replace each other to form the decision rule. Avoid obvious semantic aliases, exact complements, and deterministic transforms. That is to say, if 2 or more fields refer to exactly the same fact, or they are completly dependent on each other, for instance, mass and weight, speed and velocity, then you should reserve only one of them, eliminate the redundant fields. Each field in the final output set should be distinguishable from each other. Self check before you finally output the field inventory: - You should have brainstormed as diverse as possible to give every realistic measurement that could inform intervention tendency under the scenerio; - You should have assigned stable field_id, concise display_name, integer or decimal type, exact unit, one complete description, and pressure_direction to each field; - No field should be an alias or fully dependent on others, redundant or non-distinguishable ones have been eliminated. Figure 8: System prompt for discovering decision-relevant observable fields and their intervention directions.

sections.title: Field Semantics Prompt
sections.content: Your job is to analyze the input fields according to their description and other given information, then assign effect_strength, eligible_families and reversal semantics to each of them. You should consider the complete scenario, action ladder, field inventory, and fixed rule-family meaning. Output exactly as required, where field_id is used to refer to the given field, so do not edit or change it, otherwise you would be assigning values/texts to wrong field. Effect_strength is for the fields quantified decision relevance relative to the complete catalog, which reflects how significant the field is in affecting the final decision making compared to other fields. Assign value in [0.1, 1.0] for each field. Effect_strength regards the relative significance, that is to say, fields with effect_strength 0.1 only means that it is less severe than other fields, it does not mean the field is not important, so use the full range meaningfully to make each field more distinguishable. Eligible_families regards whether the measurement genuinely supports: graded contribution for additive aggregation, meaningful joint gate for conjunctive gating, or an independently decisive severe value for disjunctive sufficiency. Select the supported roles for each field after fully analyzing the fields role and the three supplied family meanings. Is_reversal examines whether fields impact on the intervention tendency could reverse across different conditions. For instance, "machine uptime minutes" normally means more availability and less intervention pressure, but during mandated preventive-shutdown window the same high uptime means the required outage was skipped, which requests for more intensive intervention the operating rule changed, the measurement did not. Mark is_reversal=true for such kind of fields, when there exists reasonable event that could genuinely reverses what higher value of this same unchanged measurement implies for intervention on the same action ladder. Notice that the event may be external changes; for example, in cybersecurity operations, higher outbound traffic may normally increase exfiltration concern, while during an approved backup window the same measurement can instead indicate expected backup progress and reduce intervention pressure. Also, the magnitudes of the two tendencies do not need to be similar or symmetric; any genuine nonzero opposite monotonic tendency qualifies as reversal. You must fully brainstorm the existence of such kind of reversal event before you finally assign "false". However, be aware that reverse means flip in direction on intervention tendency; change in action cost, ease, authority, or execution capability is not reversal. field that changing into meaningless, undefined or losing its impact after the trigger being activated should also not be considered as reversal. For instance, field may have pressure direction 1 (positive impact on intervention tendency), but after the event happens, field may no longer influence the urgency of taking immediate intervention, this kind of changes are not considered as reverse. For each field that you assign "is_reversal=true", you should further consider the rationale and trigger, fill all four event-fields with one concrete but consise sentence: - trigger: the concrete scenario-plausible operational event or conditional change that flips the tendency; Notice that trigger should be independent to the action decision and the fields actual value, it must not pre-decide the action or field value to make it affect the pressure direction. - semantics_before: how higher value of this unchanged measurement maps to intervention tendency in the original condition, be careful to confirm that this should agree to the given pressure direction value; - semantics_after: how the same higher observation maps to the opposite intervention tendency after the triggerred event; - reversal_reason: why the regime genuinely reverses the causal meaning of the same measurement. For is_reversal=false, set these four fields to empty strings and use reversal_rationale to explain what conditions and event were considered and tested and why the tendency should remains stable across different conditions. You should write details of what conditions and events have been tested, do not casaully or briefly skip the brainstorm just because the reverse is not obvious. For true, set reversal_rationale empty. 27 Before returning, check the following: all fields effect_strength, eligible_family, reversal semantics has been fully assigned values; effect strengths must be globally comparable; family roles must follow the fixed mathematical meanings; and every reversal account has been fully analyzed. Figure 9: System prompt for assigning field significance, eligible rule families, and direction-reversal semantics.

sections.title: Field Parameter Calibration Prompt
sections.content: You calibrate realistic synthetic numeric priors for frozen operational measurements whose decision semantics are already accepted. Jointly author legal range, typical range, and low/mixed/high Beta populations for every assigned field. Do not change field identity, measurement semantics, relative strength, family eligibility, or reversal properties. Author numerical calibration for every assigned field exactly once. Use the complete catalog to keep all batches grounded in the same ordinary, mixed, and stressed scenario populations. For each assigned field: 1. Set credible legal minimum and maximum in its frozen unit, with narrower typical range covering ordinary operation. Legal and typical ranges are different concepts. Choose the legal range around values realistically observable across the fields common and stressed scenario populations, considering the intended profile means; do not stretch it to merely theoretical extreme that makes common values occupy tiny fraction of the range. Explicitly verify minimum <= typical_range[0] <= typical_range [1] <= maximum. 2. Define low, mixed, and high intervention-tendency populations over normalized x=(vminimum)/(maximum-minimum) using Beta(alpha,beta). Each alpha and beta must be strictly greater than 0, and each concentration alpha+beta must be from 4 through 12 inclusive. The normalized mean is m=alpha/(alpha+beta), and the mapped raw mean is minimum+m*( maximum-minimum). 3. For pressure_direction=1 require m_low <= m_mixed <= m_high; for pressure_direction=-1 require m_low >= m_mixed >= m_high. The mapped raw means for both low and mixed must fall inside the authored typical range. The high center may leave the typical range when it remains plausible stressed population, but should approach legal extreme only when the scenario supports such population. 4. Choose concentrations alpha+beta that express plausible within-profile variation. Shared shapes are valid only when field semantics justify them; do not copy one universal Beta template. 5. In parameter_basis, summarize the legal/typical range basis and the population centers and variance. Treat emitted ranges and Beta pairs as numerical authority; do not restate calculated means as prose numbers. You should calculate normalized and mapped raw means for all three profiles of each field. Verify their order against the frozen pressure_direction. Write down the required inequality internally before choosing shapes: direction 1 means low <= mixed <= high; direction -1 means low >= mixed >= high. Verify both low and mixed mapped means lie inside the authored typical range, not merely inside the legal range. Then verify that parameter_basis describes those exact populations without reversing their meanings. Do not casually assign value without verification. Figure 10: System prompt for specifying realistic field ranges and Beta population parameters.

sections.title: Lexicographic Order Prompt
sections.content: Your job is to discover as many usable three-field lexicographic groups and to author the defensible first-to-last priority rules for those groups. Treat every supplied field as candidate, but do not force field into an invalid group merely to increase coverage or count. lexicographic group is set of three distinct fields that can serve as successive decision cues for the same scenario, decision objective, and action ladder. Each field must have realistic, nonempty region in which its value can independently settle an action or intervention level without being numerically combined with the other two; Each field must also have meaningful indifference or inconclusive region in which later cue can still provide residual decision evidence. In this way, the three fields [A,B,C] could form priority rule: If satisfy condition, then it directly decides the final decision, no matter what values and take; Else if satisfy condition, then it decides the final decision regardless of C; Else we make the final decision based on the value of C. The three fields should not be aliases, deterministic restatements, fields whose decision meaning depends on jointly calculating another member, mutually exclusive measurements with no realistic common decision condition, and sets for which no member can leave meaningful unresolved case to the next cue. valid group needs at least one coherent ordering, but its priority need not be inherent, universal, or the only defensible policy choice. For example, [current_collateral_shortfall_usd, settlement_failure_probability, minutes_to_settlement_cutoff] can form valid lexicographic group: material collateral shortfall may independently settle the intervention level; when the shortfall is within its indifference region, settlement-failure probability provides distinct risk cue; and when both are inconclusive, time to cutoff supplies the final urgency cue. Likewise, [vehicle_range_remaining_km, driver_duty_time_remaining_minutes, shift_time_remaining_minutes] can form valid group: critically insufficient vehicle range may require recovery on physical-feasibility grounds; when range is not decisive, insufficient legal duty time may independently require reassignment; and when neither constraint settles the case, remaining shift time provides the final operational-horizon cue. These examples illustrate how distinct fields can successively and independently determine an action without being jointly calculated. They are not fixed patterns: consider other decision roles and retain only substantively justified orderings rather than automatically emitting every permutation. Your task is to find as many distinct valid three-field groups as the catalog meaningfully supports, then determine which exact orderings of each group have scenario-grounded rationale. In an ordered rule [first, second, third], the first field settles the decision whenever it is materially decisive and otherwise passes the case to the second; the second does the same for the cases left unresolved by the first; the third supplies the final cue when both earlier fields are inconclusive. Notice that we do not require the ordering to be concrete or very obvious, because the order is rule to be established, we only require the group to be reasonable and not counterintuitive. Fields may participate in many overlapping groups, and the same unordered group may support more than one ordering. Do not partition the catalog into disjoint triples, stop after convenient number, or emit all six permutations by default without fully analyzing. Do not set up groups purely based on the fields name, you should think based on their description and actual role. You can discover the lexicographic groups with the following thinking strategy: 1. Read every fields description and identify the decision role it can independently play, such as current state or severity, consequence magnitude, likelihood, urgency or time horizon, trend or persistence, recoverability, evidence reliability, or execution feasibility. Identify both the readings that can settle an action and the readings that would leave the decision unresolved. 2. Build overlapping candidate neighborhoods around shared decision concerns and complementary decision roles. field may belong to several neighborhoods. Do not require all three fields to measure the same concept, and do not treat disagreement between their indications as incompatibility. 3. Within each neighborhood, identify strong anchor pairs: two nonredundant fields that can each independently settle some cases and can sensibly be consulted in succession without requiring joint calculation. 30 4. Expand each anchor pair with every substantively distinct third field that can resolve cases left inconclusive by the pair. Revisit strong pair with alternative third cues instead of accepting only the first plausible completion. 5. Revisit fields that are absent or rarely used. Search for additional neighborhoods, anchor pairs, and third-cue roles that connect them to the rest of the catalog, but do not force every field to belong to lexicographic group 6. Deduplicate the resulting unordered groups. For each retained group, compare the plausible first, second, and third assignments and keep only the orderings whose three positions have distinct, concrete policy roles. Similar wording with the positions permuted is not sufficient rationale. 7. Make final coverage sweep across decision roles, semantic neighborhoods, reused anchor pairs, and underused fields so that obvious valid groups are not omitted. For every retained ordered rule, output exactly three distinct supplied field IDs in firstto-last order, stable and unique order_id that distinguishes alternative orders, and one concise rationale tied to that exact sequence. Return the supported ordered triples in the required flat output format; do not output intermediate neighborhoods, anchor pairs, unordered-group records, quotas, or unsupported permutations. Figure 11: System prompt for deriving admissible three-field priority orders for lexicographic decision rules. 31 Cross-Field Constraint Prompt Your job is to compare against different fields and author executable cross-field feasibility constraints according to their definition. First identify fields connected by strong definitional, accounting, population-containment, or physical-capacity relationship. Emit constraint only when their jointly observed numeric values must satisfy that relation, the constraint should be some hard restriction to avoid value combinations that is obviously impossible in real world. For instance, the combination "total_number_of_objects = 30" and "number_of_type_A_object = 40" may be impossible if type object belongs to total objects, union cannot be less than/smaller than its part. Ordinary correlation, causal expectation, common co-movement , and typical behavior are not invariants; an empty list is valid. Evaluate constraint only over records where every field it references has numeric value. Only consider cross field relations and constraints, do not encode availability, nullness, missingness, benign non-applicability, or single-field legal ranges in the expression, and never use fields ordinary range bound as guard for cross-field relation. Prefer one direct comparison whenever it states the invariant. When genuine conditional invariant is needed, use implies explicitly instead of using an equivalent expression of or. Express each invariant with the finite structured expression grammar. numeric atom is {" field": FIELD_ID}. numeric term is an atom, {"const": NUMBER}, or one arithmetic node over atoms; add and mul take two to eight atoms, while sub and div take exactly two. numeric expression is term or one arithmetic node over terms with the same arities. comparison uses leltgegteq with numeric-expression left and right. Boolean clause is comparison, not of one comparison, or andor over two to eight comparisons. complete Boolean expression is clause, not of one clause, andor over two to eight clauses, or implies whose if and then are clauses. Do not nest beyond these layers. Split independent conjuncts into separate constraints instead of nesting repeated and nodes. All arithmetic and comparisons must be dimensionally valid. Operands of add and sub must have compatible dimensions, and the two sides of every comparison must have compatible dimensions after any explicit exact unit conversion. mul and div may be used only when their resulting dimensions make the comparison valid. Never directly compare count with rate or duration. constraint can be set among more than 2 fields, for each candidate, verify only the actual definitions to establish the constraint, do not judge merely from the field name. If any valid joint numeric assignment can violate the proposed relation, omit it. Notice that independent constraints should be established separately, thus long constraints are used only when necessary, do not combine several short constraints into whole long expression. Before returning, compare all retained constraints. If constraint contains could be devide into two or more independent constraints, then split them. If two constraints impose the same restriction after commutative reordering or algebraic simplification, emit only the clearer, shallower one. Do not treat partial overlap or one-way implication as duplication. Give each retained constraint stable id and one concise description stating why the numeric restriction is necessary. Every constraint must have non-empty ID that is unique within feasibility_constraints. Never reuse an ID for two constraints, even when their descriptions or expressions differ. Before returning, confirm that every field reference is one supplied ID and evaluate the exact AST on its boundary cases to ensure it states the same restriction as the description. Similar names alone do not establish equality, complementarity, containment, or interchangeability. Figure 12: System prompt for constructing executable cross-field feasibility constraints.

sections.title: Field Replacement Prompt
sections.content: Your job is to inspect the complete frozen field inventory and find every two-field replacement supported by coherent event. Do not preselect by similar names, identical units, or an assumption that replacements must naturally occupy exactly the same status. replacement means that concrete scenario-plausible event or condition change can make one field reasonably take the other fields place in the same rule slot. The two measurements do not need to be identical, interchangeable in every situation, or equally authoritative before and after the event. They need defensible reason why the incoming field becomes the more appropriate cue when the outgoing field stops occupying that slot. Retain pair only when both fields have the same frozen pressure_direction , so the handoff preserves the slots intervention meaning. Different types, units, and raw constructs are allowed and are not rejection criteria. Consider every field pair in both directions. Keep pair whenever you can explain concrete handoff event that: - makes the outgoing field unavailable, stale, out of scope, less representative, or no longer the preferred evidence for that rule position; and - makes the incoming field available and relevant enough to take that position without contradicting the intervention meaning of the outgoing field. Do not require the incoming field to reproduce exactly the same quantity, population, horizon, or evidentiary status. Those differences may be the reason replacement becomes useful. Exclude pair only when the frozen meanings have incompatible intervention implications in the claimed circumstances, the two fields must necessarily be used together rather than one taking the others slot, or no coherent event can justify the handoff. Classify the relationship according to the actual rationale: - same_metric: alternate sources report the same construct with the same frozen pressure direction; - different_horizon: compatible measurements describe the same construct at different horizons or observation cutoffs with the same frozen pressure direction; - same_source: distinct views from one governing system can replace one another after workflow or authority change; - proxy_substitution: different constructs can occupy the same rule position under different conditions because each is reasonable proxy for the decision concern then relevant. Raw types and units may differ, but the frozen pressure direction must remain the same. For each retained group, output unique group_id; the two members; the honest relation_type; concise decision_role naming their shared rule function; pairspecific rationale explaining the shared decision concern, the meaningful difference between the measurements, and why that difference still permits the event-specific handoff; concise source_contrast; exactly one authority_by_field entry for each member; coupling_strength from 0 through 0.6 representing expected normalized dependence; the effective_scope; and the two directed transitions required below. effective_scope must describe the governed business objects or population, workflow or decision boundary, and relevant time or authority boundary within which the handoff applies. It is not list of rule families or field eligibility labels. Do not let rationale merely restate that one field becomes unavailable and the other becomes available. Author exactly two directed transitions, one in each direction. Each direction needs its own plausible trigger, reason the outgoing field relinquishes the slot, reason the incoming field can take it, an expected duration, and an ending condition. The two directions may rely on different events and need not be symmetric or equally common. transition is invalid only when it removes the outgoing field but provides no positive reason for using the incoming field. Return all supported groups found by the complete pairwise sweep. Fields may participate in multiple groups. capacity_findings should briefly record the search and concrete nearcandidates that truly lacked any coherent handoff; an empty replacement list requires specific evidence that the strongest candidate pairs were considered. 33 Figure 13: System prompt for specifying event-grounded field replacements and their directional transitions.

sections.title: Candidate Semantic Review Prompt
sections.content: You audit candidate decision episodes for real-world coherence. Treat every candidate independently. Judge whether the declared rule roles and all eight visible measurements can coexist for the same governed entity, decision time, and horizon. For replacement and reversal candidates, assess only the declared operation; do not invent an event, rationale, or additional rule change. Use reject_core when the relevant field roles or declared operation are incoherent. Use reject_distractors only when the core is coherent but the distractor set cannot coexist with it or leaks post-decision outcome. Use accept when the core and complete visible field set are coherent. Do not propose replacement fields. candidate with prior_core_review has already passed its core review: judge only its newly drawn distractors and return only reject_distractors or accept. Return only the strict JSON object requested by the response schema. Figure 14: System prompt for reviewing candidate episode field configurations, rule changes, and distractors. 35 Dataset-Level Quality Review Prompt You are the final semantic quality reviewer for dynamic decision-rule dataset. Score every supplied episode independently on all three dimensions from 0.0 to 5.0 in increments of 0.1. Use the full scale: 5 is exemplary, 4 is strong, 3 is acceptable with visible weaknesses, 2 is substantially weak, 1 has severe problem, and 0 is incoherent or contradictory. field_realism measures whether the eight fields can naturally be available for the stated decision, governed entity, time, and horizon, and whether the field combination fits the scenario. rule_change_realism measures whether the stated trigger_event and change_reason plausibly produce the exact replacement and direction reversal shown by the pre/post core fields and directions. compound change must follow from one coherent observable operational event rather than two unrelated events. distractor_quality measures whether distractors are plausible, superficially relevant context without directly encoding the action, leaking the outcome, or semantically subsuming the rule core. Do not penalize distractor merely for being correlated with the decision or occasionally seeming important in randomly sampled case; penalize it only when its definition clearly dominates, duplicates, or bypasses the intended core mechanism. Give exactly one concise sentence (at most 240 characters) explaining each dimension score. Return every episode_id exactly once using only the requested JSON schema. Figure 15: System prompt for scoring field realism, rule-change realism, and distractor quality in dynamic episodes.

sections.title: Initial Prompt
sections.content: ===== System message ===== # Role <role: one sentence assigning the domain decision task> Choose one of the four actions for every case. Your objective is to maximize Cumulative Utility the total utility earned by submitted actions. Probes reveal information about the hidden rule. When choosing probe cases, avoid redundant probes, such as repeating the same case or using cases whose field values are nearly identical. The decision rule may or may not change during the episode. You are not told if or when it changes; change can only happen right after you complete an action batch. # Actions - **<action display name>** (action_0): <what this action does in the domain> - **<action display name>** (action_1): <what this action does in the domain> - **<action display name>** (action_2): <what this action does in the domain> - **<action display name>** (action_3): <what this action does in the domain> # Field relevance Some listed fields are distractors. Only subset affects the hidden rule and utility; changing the other fields cannot change utility. The relevant subset is hidden, so infer it from probe results and action feedback. It may change if the decision rule changes during the episode. # Rule family The hidden rule uses exactly one of these four families: - additive_aggregation: combine weighted contributions from relevant fields. - conjunctive_gating: all conditions matter; the weakest condition controls. - disjunctive_sufficiency: any sufficient condition can control; the strongest condition controls. - lexicographic_priority: inspect fields in priority order; the first decisive field controls, otherwise fall back to the last field. Infer the family from probe results and action feedback. The family name and field roles are not given directly. # Utility scale Each submitted action receives per-case utility from fixed four-action mapping. Utilities are not normalized to [-1, 1]: across the full score range, an individual utility is approximately between -0.33 and 0.98. The theoretical lower and upper limits are about -0.333 and 0.976. Positive utility is better, negative utility is worse, and 0 is neutral; the four utilities for one case sum to approximately 0. Abstaining also receives utility 0, but is counted as incorrect. Maximize the sum of utilities across submitted actions. # Reply format Every reply is exactly one JSON object with two keys, tool and arguments, and nothing else no prose, Markdown, rationale, or extra keys. Example: json {"tool":"request_next_batch","arguments":{}} 37 Use only tool marked available in the latest tool_usability; an accepted call is final. # Tools ## probe_batch look at example cases before deciding Each probe shows one case and the utility of all four actions on it. Probe results are information only and earn no utility; action feedback exposes only the per-case utility of the actions you submitted. Two probe forms. fresh case give value for every field in raw_field_schema: json {"tool":"probe_batch","arguments":{"probes":[{"values":{"<field_id>":1}}]}} variation of known case start from context ID returned by probe feedback and edit some of its fields: json {"tool":"probe_batch","arguments":{"probes":[{"base_context_id":"<context_id>","changes ":{}}]}} Limits: one probe_batch call per batch window, at most 16 probes per call. Respect field types, feasibility constraints, and two-decimal precision for decimals. Probe policy: submit at least one valid probe when you choose probe_batch. ## request_next_batch reveal the next batch without probing json {"tool":"request_next_batch","arguments":{}} ## submit_action_batch answer the pending cases json {"tool":"submit_action_batch","arguments":{"batch_id":"batch_01","actions":{"<context_id>":" action_1"}}} pending_action_batch lists 8 context IDs; give at most one action for each. You may omit IDs to abstain abstained cases receive utility 0 and count as incorrect and actions may even be empty. ## calculator optional arithmetic helper json {"tool":"calculator","arguments":{"expressions":["total = (12.5+3)*4","sqrt(total)"]}} Pure arithmetic: numbers, operators, parentheses, and the functions abs, sqrt, min, max, sum, mean, round, floor, ceil, log, log10, exp, pow. name = expression assigns variable and returns its value, and within one call you may reference variable before its assignment appears. Variables are call-local: to reuse value in later call, copy the number into the new expression. After calculator call, use different tool before calculating again two calculator calls in row are not allowed. # Batch flow 1. Batch 1 is hidden. Call probe_batch or request_next_batch to reveal it. 2. When pending_action_batch exists, call submit_action_batch; otherwise 38 choose probe_batch or request_next_batch. 3. After each submitted batch except the last, again choose probe_batch or request_next_batch before the next batch. 4. rejected call gets one repair opportunity. If the second call is invalid, hidden batch is revealed by skipping probe; pending action batch fails with every case unanswered at utility 0, and the environment advances to the next window. 5. Use the latest state card as authoritative. Do not infer hidden rules or metadata from identifiers. # State and history After you complete an action batch, the environment rewrites retained history before the next request: the revealed cases, your submit_action_batch call, and your action-solving messages are removed, and an environment-authored outcome replaces them. The next message opens like this: Environment result: { "message": "The environment accepted action batch 3. Your selected actions and actionsolving messages are hidden from later agent context.", "batch_number": 3, "results": [{"context_id": "case_017", "utility": 0.59}, {"context_id": "case_018", " utility": -0.31}], "batch_utility": 1.33, "cumulative_utility": 5.62, "cumulative_probes": 8 } This outcome means the named batch was just hidden, and it is your only record of that round. Treat it as scoreboard for your induced rule: each utility is the payoff of the action you chose, so high utilities confirm the rule and low or negative ones flag mismatches. If batch scores markedly worse than earlier batches under the same hypothesis, your rule is wrong or the rule changed after the previous batch consider whether additional probing would help. Only context IDs returned by probe feedback may be used as bases for incremental probes; use complete values for new probe. The initial user message contains field descriptions and Current state card. Later messages contain an Environment result followed by the latest card. Use the latest card for tool usability, cumulative_utility, cumulative_probes, pending cases, and remaining action batches; use conversation history for earlier probe/action evidence. ===== First user message ===== Input fields: Every field below is numeric probe input and is required in full values probe. Use JSON numbers only: integer requires whole number and decimal accepts an integer or decimal number. null, strings, and booleans are invalid, even when field description discusses an unavailable real-world observation. - **<field display name>** (<field_id>, type: <integer or decimal>, unit: <unit>): <field description> ... one bullet per field ... Current state: { "cumulative_utility": 0, "cumulative_probes": 0, "remaining_action_batches": 12, "pending_action_batch": null, "tool_usability": [ { "tool": "probe_batch", "available": true, "reason": null }, { "tool": "request_next_batch", "available": true, "reason": null }, { "tool": "submit_action_batch", "available": false, "reason": "no action batch is pending; reveal one with probe_batch or request_next_batch first" }, { "tool": "calculator", "available": true, "reason": null } ] } Figure 16: The initial prompt under Default. The system message is identical across episodes, and angle brackets mark the episode-specific role, action, and field descriptions. The first user message closes with the initial Current state card.
